title: Lectio divina, 4: rest
hookLine: stop talking and rest in what's been given

lines: THE END OF A LONG TALK.
cards: Late at night, at the end of a long talk between old friends, a moment can come when everything that needed saying has been said. Nobody reaches for a phone. Nobody fills the quiet.
Two people just sit together, and the silence isn't empty. A grandparent holding a sleeping baby knows a quiet like that too. Guigo's ladder ends there.
After reading, chewing and answering, the fourth rung isn't another thing to do. It's the moment you stop doing.

teach.b: First, the word. Contemplatio, Latin for contemplation. It came up four days ago, with the farmer at Ars: I look at him, he looks at me.
Now you can see where it sits: at the top of Guigo's ladder. Reading seeks, meditation finds, prayer asks, contemplation tastes.
Guigo treats it as a rung you can't climb by trying: while the soul is still asking, he says, God interrupts the prayer and comes to meet it.
Second, a gift, not an achievement. The Catechism calls contemplation a gift, a grace: it can't be made to happen, only made room for. Read, chew, answer, then be quiet.
In Catholic teaching, the rest is God's part. Some days that silence is full. Some days it's just quiet, and that's fine too.
Third, the model. Luke tells of two sisters, Martha and Mary, welcoming Jesus. Martha is busy serving; Mary sits at his feet, listening.

teach.h: MARY HATH CHOSEN THE BEST PART.
teach.b: When Martha complains, Jesus answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "But one thing is necessary. Mary hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her."
Martha isn't the villain here; the Church honors her as a saint too. But there's a time to sit. Fourth, the verse's last promise: I will refresh you.
In Greek, the word means I will give you rest.
You came burdened. You read, you chewed, you answered. Now you rest, like the weaned child in the psalm from camp four, quiet against its mother.
Not asleep. Just close, and still.

how: Catholics who practice lectio divina end it with a few minutes of silence, simply resting in God's presence, and some monasteries and parishes keep times of silent prayer after the readings.

o: the hardest prayer, kept for monks and saints
resting quietly with God once the words run out
thinking deeply about a hard question of faith

games.q: climb the whole ladder — tap the pairs.

s: you can reach contemplation by trying harder
the tradition calls it a gift. you can only make room for it.
Jesus tells Martha that Mary has chosen the best part
"Mary hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her."
the Greek word behind I will refresh you means I will give you rest
Matthew 11:28: come, all you who are burdened, and I will give you rest.

games.q: you're Martha. Jesus is in your house, there's a meal to get ready, and your sister is just sitting at his feet. you complain. what does he say?
o: tell Mary to get up and help.
Mary has chosen the best part.
don't worry about the meal; I'll make bread.
games.why: "But one thing is necessary. Mary hath chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her." there's a time to sit.

practice: Say the verse one last time: come to me, all you that labor, and are burdened, and I will refresh you.

Then stop, and for two minutes sit without words: don't chew, don't answer, don't plan, just sit the way you'd sit with an old friend at the end of the night, and let thoughts pass like cars on a far-off road.
If you pray, simply rest in God's company; if you don't, rest in the quiet itself.

wordCard.voice: Contemplatio. The fourth rung: after reading, chewing and answering, you stop, and rest in what's been given. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: I will give rest, the word behind I will refresh you in Matthew 11:28.

carryVoice: Your line: rest in it. The top rung isn't climbed; it's given. See you tomorrow.
